newsitem.title: UK: Dlr/yen firms in Europe but tight ranges persist.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/yen firms in Europe but tight ranges persist.

text.p: The dollar crept higher against the yen in early Europe, bolstered by a firm mark against the yen but still kept within fairly narrow ranges across the board amid a dearth of fresh factors.

Dealers said the dollar was sidelined amid caution before the weekend G7 meeting and with the focus on events in Europe, particularly French President Jacques Chirac's decision to go for an early election.
Although the mark was steady to slightly easier on its European crosses, the uncertainty the French election brings to monetary union progress is seen as mark supportive.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said late Monday that an EMU delay could be considered if big countries were to miss the convergence criteria. In an earlier speech, however, Tietmeyer said the Bundesbank was working on the assumption of a timely EMU start.
"Tietmeyer is underlining the central bank's desire for strict interpretation of the criteria and has raised the issue that a delay is better than a fudge," said a U.S. bank dealer.
Germany's six leading economic institutes said in their spring report today they forecast the German 1997 budget deficit to be 3.0-3.2 percent of GDP.
Dollar/mark rose slightly after the German institutes said they saw the dollar averaging 1.80 marks in 1998.
However, Bundesbank member Franz-Christoph Zeitler said today said the necessity for major currencies to correct against the mark was now over.
By 0805 GMT, dollar/mark was trading at 1.7064/71 against 1.7034/41 late Monday in Europe.

The dollar was firmer against the yen, climbing above 126 yen but dealers said there was wariness to push higher ahead of the weekend G7 and Friday's meeting between Japan Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and U.S. President Bill Clinton.
The dollar was trading at 126.17/22 yen from 125.58/63 yen late Monday in Europe.
Dollar/yen was bolstered by gains in mark/yen, currently at 73.88/91 after touching an earlier high of 73.97. It stood at 73.78/80 late Monday.
"We think the G7 is going to be slightly bearish for the dollar," said Tom Rayner, international economist at Societe General Strauss Turnbull in London.
"We may get a slightly firmer message (than Berlin G7), they don't want to be seen to be ignored by the market."
Japan's Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said overnight the views on forex agreed at February's G7 meeting in Berlin are likely to remain unchanged at the weekend meeting in Washington.
The G7 in Berlin expressed its view that forex rates should reflect fundamentals and excessive volatility is undesirable, stopping short of endorsing central bank intervention.
